extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, law students, judges and patent agents (Canadian patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for determining obviousness/inventiveness of patent claims under Canadian law (Sanofi/Windsurfing framework and related doctrines). Focuses on how to set up the inquiry, evidentiary considerations, statutory constraints, and indicia of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing / Sanofi four-step approach
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-step approach to determine obviousness: (1) identify the notional 'person skilled in the art' and their relevant common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept of the claim or, if that cannot readily be done, construe the claim; (3) identify differences between the state of the art and the inventive concept/claim as construed; (4) viewed without knowledge of the alleged invention, do those differences constitute steps which would have been obvious to the person skilled in the art or require any degree of invention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada (Sanofi). The Court warned against an overly rigid application; the approach is useful and flexible. Failure to recite the exact words is not necessarily error; use as a structured inquiry rather than a compulsory formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (posita)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the notional 'person skilled in the art' (a paragon of deduction and dexterity, 'devoid of inventiveness or imagination').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define their skills, typical training and experience; this hypothetical person's perspective is the benchmark for obviousness. Experts help establish what would have been available to this person, but the ultimate decision is for the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common general knowledge of the skilled person
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the relevant common general knowledge of the person skilled in the art (facts or skills known and available to all in the field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common general knowledge can include everyday skills (2+2 example) and things that change over time; courts may consider later-published art as evidence of what was commonly known at the relevant time. Distinguish common general knowledge from public but obscure prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify inventive concept or properly construe the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the inventive concept of the claim in question or, if not readily discernible, construe the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanofi step two; for combination patents, proper claim construction may suffice because the essence often lies in the unique combination claimed rather than a paraphrase of the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare differences between prior art and inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what, if any, differences exist between the matter cited as forming part of the state of the art and the inventive concept of the claim or the claim as construed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the third step in Windsurfing/Sanofi; clearly list distinguishing features to assess whether they require invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness assessed without knowledge of the alleged invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewed without any knowledge of the alleged invention as claimed, determine whether the identified differences would have been obvious to the skilled person or require invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanofi step four; avoids hindsight bias by asking whether the skilled person, lacking the inventor's insight, would arrive at the invention directly and without difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory s.28.3 test: subject-matter of the claim on the claim date
rubrics_metrics.description: Under s.28.3 of the Patent Act, the subject-matter defined by a claim must be subject-matter that would not have been obvious on the claim date to a person skilled in the art, having regard to specified prior disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test focuses on the subject-matter defined by the claim (not necessarily the inventive concept as framed in Sanofi). Consider disclosure by applicant >1 year before filing and disclosures by others before the claim date. Apply to the claim as filed/constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness is a question of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is characterized as a question of fact to be decided by the trier of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although experts will often testify, the court determines obviousness based on evidence, sound judgment and reason. Expert opinion assists but cannot replace the court's decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper subject-matter: combination vs aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between proper subject-matter: combinations (which may be patentable) versus mere aggregations (which are not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the invention is a new combination of steps/ideas or simply a collection of old ones. For combination inventions, avoid dissecting and judging only the parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dissecting combinations into parts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to dissect a claimed combination into constituent parts and assess obviousness of each part separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claimed invention is the combination; breaking it down risks improper invalidation when the inventive leap lies in the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosaicing / combining multiple prior art sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilled person may combine multiple pieces of prior art (including public but not commonly known documents) to arrive at the invention, but courts should examine closely why such a combination would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible when references are linked (one referring to another) or would be found in routine literature searches. Courts scrutinize such combinations to guard against hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation / climate of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider motivation in the field: attitudes, trends, prejudices, expectations; and the motivation of the inventor or the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include whether others were moving in the same direction, prejudices for/against making the invention, and whether there was a recognized problem motivating work in the area. Motivation in prior art is also relevant under Sanofi factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try / predictability (Sanofi 'obvious to try' test)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions borne of experimentation, determine whether it was 'more or less self-evident' that the approach would work, whether there were a finite number of identified predictable solutions, and the nature/amount of effort required (routine vs prolonged and arduous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanofi factors: (1) self-evident it ought to work; (2) finite/predictable solutions; (3) routine trials vs prolonged effort; (4) motivation in the prior art. 'Mere possibility' is not enough; high predictability is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite number of identified predictable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the 'obvious to try' analysis: whether there was a finite number of known or predictable solutions to try.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the skilled person faced many unpredictable options, 'obvious to try' is less likely to support obviousness. If only a few predictable options existed, the test may favor obviousness if trials were routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and amount of effort required
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the work required routine trials or prolonged and arduous experimentation to achieve the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant, unpredictable, or prolonged experimentation favors non-obviousness (inventive); routine, straightforward efforts favor obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable / sufficiently predictable results are obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If results were sufficiently predictable or 'self-evident' that an approach would work, the invention may be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require more than a mere possibility; predictability of success is a key indicator especially in chemical/pharmaceutical cases (Pfizer/Viagra discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmatory and predictable experiments are not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmatory experiments that merely follow instructions or predictions of others, or that yield predictable results, are not inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following instructions or the predictions of prior art does not create inventive ingenuity; confirmatory work that only validates expected outcomes is not patentable invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cripps question: led directly and without difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Would the skilled person, in the light of the state of the art and common general knowledge at the relevant date, have come 'directly and without difficulty' to the claimed solution?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strict test often quoted in cases; if answer is 'Yes' the invention is obvious. Related to 'plain as day' / 'crystal clear' formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Path vs result: inventor's actual route
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of the inventor's actual path is of limited relevance; some authorities focus only on results not how they were achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts differ: some consider the number of decisions/choices required (path matters), others say the court is concerned only with the results and not the way the conquest was achieved (I.G. Farben). The path may be used as empirical evidence but is not determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex post facto / 20-20 hindsight caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ex post facto analysis which renders every invention obvious after the fact; hindsight is the most dangerous factor and must be applied with care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unfair to select a few prior art documents post hoc when one knows what to look for. Expert testimony asserting 'I could have done that' requires explanation why they did not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (commercial success, awards, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary factors such as commercial success and meritorious awards may be used as indicia of non-obviousness/inventive ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are instructive but their weight depends on evidence and context; courts treat them as supplementary and not determinative alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequently recognized advantages have limited weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages of the invention recognized after the claim date are of limited usefulness in assessing obviousness at the claim date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later-appreciated benefits should generally be given little weight when assessing inventive ingenuity as of the relevant date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and role of expert witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert evidence is necessary to explain the relevant skills of the hypothetical skilled person and the state of the art, but experts cannot simply instruct the court whether the invention is obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best experts are 'good teachers' who explain opinions simply. Courts evaluate experts' credibility and must reach the obviousness conclusion themselves; expert assertions need to be supported by explanations addressing why others did or did not arrive at the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and public knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether prior art was accessible or would have been found by routine literature searches; public but obscure documents may still be combined if reasonably accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One document referring to another may make referral obvious; the court examines how a skilled person would find or be alerted to such documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Sanofi with flexibility to New Act patents but focus on claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanofi's test can be applied to 'New Act' (s.28.3) patents but the statute emphasizes assessing the 'subject-matter defined by a claim'; courts have reconciled Sanofi with claim-focused analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where claims are properly construed (especially combination claims), determining inventive concept may be unnecessary; still ensure the obviousness inquiry respects statutory language limiting consideration to claim subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests that are improper or insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain shorthand formulations are unreliable alone: 'worth a try', mere routine testing, or later-recognized advantages are inadequate tests of inventive ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have deprecated simplistic tests; apply the structured Sanofi/Windsurfing factors and guard against over-simplified conclusions.
